title: Scrum in Plain English: Empiricism, Value and a Self-Managing Team
summary: Understand Scrum as a lightweight framework built on transparency, inspection and adaptation rather than as a task-tracking process.
plain_language_explanation: Scrum creates short feedback loops around a product goal. The Scrum Team uses transparency, inspection and adaptation to learn what delivers value and adjusts its plan without abandoning quality or accountability.

title: Scrum Accountabilities, Values and Events
summary: Apply the Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers accountabilities together with the five Scrum values and the purpose of each event.
body_outline: Treat Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers as accountabilities within one Scrum Team rather than command-and-control roles.
Use commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage to support empiricism.
Use Sprint Planning to establish why the Sprint is valuable, what can be done and how work will be accomplished.
Use the Daily Scrum to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan.
Use Sprint Review to inspect the outcome with stakeholders and adapt the Product Backlog.
Use Sprint Retrospective to improve quality and effectiveness.

title: Artifacts and Commitments: Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done
summary: Use Scrum artifacts and their commitments to create transparency, focus and quality without freezing scope unnecessarily.
body_outline: Use the Product Backlog and Product Goal to make long-term direction transparent.
Use the Sprint Backlog and Sprint Goal to provide focus while allowing Developers to adapt the plan.
Use the Increment and Definition of Done to make quality expectations explicit.
Do not present incomplete work as Done at Sprint Review.
Refine Product Backlog items as needed without turning refinement into a mandatory Scrum event.
Optimize for a valuable usable Increment rather than story-point output alone.

title: Professional Scrum: Coaching, Flow, Value and Anti-patterns
summary: Diagnose weak Scrum implementations using empiricism, flow, value evidence and clear accountability rather than adding more ceremony.
architecture_notes: Professional Scrum is not compliance with meetings. Strong teams make goals and quality transparent, inspect real outcomes, adapt based on evidence, reduce impediments and preserve self-management. Evidence-Based Management can complement Scrum by measuring value and the ability to deliver value rather than rewarding local output metrics.
anti_patterns: Scrum Master acts as team manager or task dispatcher
Product Owner is a committee without clear accountability
Sprint Goal is missing or merely lists backlog items
Definition of Done is weakened to inflate velocity
Sprint Review becomes a status meeting
Daily Scrum becomes a report to a manager
unfinished work is carried forward while still counted as Done
velocity is treated as a productivity target

title: Read-Only Scrum Health Evidence Pack
summary: Review one Scrum Team's goals, events, artifacts and evidence without changing backlog priorities, team accountabilities or sprint commitments.
steps: Confirm current Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done.
Review Product Backlog and Sprint Backlog transparency without reprioritizing work.
Review evidence that each Scrum event serves its inspection/adaptation purpose.
Check whether stakeholders receive usable Increments and meaningful Sprint Reviews.
Look for impediments, excessive work in progress, carry-over and quality debt.
Record hypotheses and coaching opportunities; do not alter sprint scope or accountabilities in the lab.
expected_result: A neutral evidence pack showing where Scrum supports or obstructs empiricism, value and quality without changing the team's live process.

title: Scrum Anti-pattern Decision Tree
summary: Diagnose weak outcomes by inspecting goals, transparency, quality, feedback and accountability before prescribing process changes.
diagnostic_order: Clarify the observed outcome problem before blaming a Scrum event or individual.
Check whether Product Goal, Sprint Goal and Definition of Done are understood and useful.
Inspect whether the artifacts are transparent enough to support decisions.
Check whether the Scrum Team is genuinely self-managing and accountabilities are clear.
Inspect feedback latency, stakeholder participation, quality debt and recurring impediments.
Change practices only when evidence shows how the adjustment should improve value, quality or learning.

title: Scrum Foundations Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering accountabilities, events, artifacts, commitments and empiricism.

assessment_items.question: Who can change the Sprint Backlog plan during the Sprint?
assessment_items.answer: The Developers adapt the Sprint Backlog as more is learned, collaborating with the Product Owner on scope when needed while preserving the Sprint Goal.

assessment_items.question: Can incomplete work be presented as Done in the Sprint Review?
assessment_items.answer: No. Work that does not meet the Definition of Done is not part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration.

assessment_items.question: What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum?
assessment_items.answer: Developers inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt their plan for the next day of work.

assessment_items.question: Does high velocity prove high value?
assessment_items.answer: No. Scrum focuses on valuable outcomes and usable Increments; velocity is not a Scrum value metric or productivity target.

title: Senior Scrum Interview: Empiricism, Product Value and Coaching
summary: Senior scenarios testing Scrum accountabilities, self-management, stakeholder feedback, quality and anti-pattern diagnosis.

questions.question: A manager assigns tasks during the Daily Scrum. What do you challenge?
answer_points: preserve transparency without turning event into status reporting

questions.question: A team completes many items but stakeholders see little value. What evidence do you inspect?
